common_name: China Doll Rose (Dwarf Pink Cluster-Flowered Polyantha)

planting.note: Plant container roses in late winter through spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; China Doll, a 1946 dwarf polyantha, stays low and compact, useful for edging and low borders.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; China Doll, introduced in 1946, is a dwarf polyantha bearing dense clusters of small, double, clear pink flowers on a low, tidy, mounding plant that stays under 18 inches, making it an excellent choice for edging, low borders, and mass plantings where full-size roses would overwhelm the space. It blooms nearly continuously from late spring through frost with minimal deadheading needed, since the small clustered flowers are inconspicuous once spent. Like other polyantha roses it is exceptionally low-maintenance and disease-resistant compared to hybrid teas, needing only light pruning in late winter to maintain its compact shape.

common_name: Excelsa Rambler Rose (Red Dorothy Perkins, Crimson Cluster-Flowered Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence or arbor; introduced in 1909, Excelsa is often called Red Dorothy Perkins for its similar rambling habit in a deeper crimson color.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy fence, arbor, or pergola. Excelsa, introduced in 1909 and often nicknamed Red Dorothy Perkins for its close resemblance to that classic rambler, produces enormous single-flush clusters of small, double, deep crimson-red flowers that cover its long, flexible canes each summer. Like its pink counterpart it is somewhat prone to powdery mildew, especially with poor air circulation, but its dramatic, once-yearly floral display on a large structure has kept it a favorite for historic and cottage-style gardens. Prune only to control size or remove dead wood right after the summer bloom, since it flowers on the previous year's growth and pruning at other times sacrifices next season's flowers.

common_name: Seven Sisters Rose (Antique Multiflora Rambler with Shifting Colors)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun on a large, sturdy structure; Seven Sisters, introduced from Japan in 1817, is an extremely vigorous heirloom rambler long grown across the Deep South.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a large, sturdy fence, tree, or outbuilding for support, since Seven Sisters is an exceptionally vigorous rambler capable of climbing 15-20 feet or more once established. Introduced from Japan in 1817 and long naturalized across the Deep South, it takes its name from the way each large cluster of small flowers opens in several different shades at once — from deep pink-purple in bud to pale lilac-pink and nearly white as the flowers age — so a single spray can show seven or more distinct tones simultaneously. It blooms once in a spectacular, heavy spring flush, then rests for the remainder of the season, and is remarkably tough, drought-tolerant, and long-lived once established, often found thriving around old homesites with no care at all. Prune only to control size and remove dead wood right after the spring bloom.
